## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dhūmakārijātaka* (Ja 413) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection. The narrative opening relates that the Buddha delivered the teaching while residing at Jetavana, on account of the King of Kosala favoring newcomers over his veteran troops [Fausböll 1883]. When a frontier revolt broke out, neither the neglected veterans nor the privileged newcomers fought, resulting in military defeat; the remorseful king subsequently approached the Buddha to inquire if any ruler had ever suffered a similar fate from such an error.

In the story of the past, King Yudhiṭṭhila (Koravya) poses a question to his wise minister Vidhūrapaṇḍita (the Bodhisatta) [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. To illustrate that sorrow stems from rejecting old loyalties for strangers, the Bodhisatta recounts the story of Dhūmakāri, a brāhmaṇa goatherd of the Vāsiṭṭha clan [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. Dhūmakāri tended his flock in the forest with a smoky fire to deter gnats, but upon encountering a herd of golden deer, he lavished all his care upon the deer while neglecting his goats, causing them to perish [Cowell 1897]. Once the autumn rains passed and the gnats dispersed, the deer returned to the mountains and river springs, leaving Dhūmakāri destitute, jaundiced with grief, and mourning alone [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. Hearing this tale, the king restored favor to his own people and practiced generosity [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. In the birth identification (*samodhāna*), King Koravya is identified as Ānanda, Dhūmakāri as King Pasenadi of Kosala, and Vidhūrapaṇḍita as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].

Textual reuse data compiled by DharmaNexus confirms extensive overlap between the canonical verses and the commentary, sharing six matching passages with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. In addition, DharmaNexus records cross-language alignments with Haribhaṭṭa's *Jātakamālā* (*haribhaṭṭajātakamālā-nāma*, D4152) preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur [DharmaNexus].
